subtype: Approach: assuming grandparents will handle childcare [Pitfall]
passage: Suraj and Kishore never really asked. When the baby was due in the spring, they told each other that the grandparents would simply move into the flat for a few months, the way it had always been in the family. In April, on a call from Nagpur, Suraj's mother said her knees and the house made a long stay impossible, and Suraj's father agreed. Silence. The couple had no nanny's name, no crèche form, no leave application. That week they rang around, waited in office corridors with phones pressed to their ears, and paid an agency fee they had never budgeted for. It worked out, roughly. But nobody slept, and Kishore said quietly, "We should have asked before we assumed."

qa.q: What reason did Suraj's mother give on the call?
qa.a: She said her knees and the house made a long stay impossible.

qa.q: How did Kishore feel after the call, and what shows it?
qa.a: Kishore felt regretful and uneasy, shown by the quiet remark, "We should have asked before we assumed."

qa.q: What could the couple have done earlier?
qa.a: They could have asked the grandparents early on what help was really possible and drawn up backups such as a crèche or nanny list, so nothing rested on an assumption.

qa.q: How might Suraj's parents have felt when they had to explain?
qa.a: They may have felt guilty about letting the couple down, while still needing to be honest about their limits.

grounding: Suraj and Kishore assume the grandparents will move in, and scramble with no plan when they cannot.

subtype: Approach: assuming grandparents will handle childcare [Pitfall]
passage:
"Papa, it's two months till the baby. When are you and Mummy moving in? We've cleared the second room."
Pankaj put down his tea. "Siddharth, we never said we were moving in."
"But... we assumed. Everyone's parents do."
"Your mother's back has been bad since winter. She can barely stand for an hour. And who looks after this house? Your Dadi's old things, the tenants downstairs?"
Siddharth looked at Nandita. She had gone pale. "We've already told my office I'm back at work after three months."
"Beta, I'm sorry. We'll visit often. But living there, full time, with a newborn? We can't."
In the car, Nandita said nothing for a long time. Then: "We have no plan. No crèche, no nanny, nothing. Two months."
Siddharth gripped the steering wheel. They'd never asked. They'd just assumed.

qa.q: How long did Siddharth's mother's back trouble last?
qa.a: It had been bad since winter.

qa.q: How did Nandita feel in the car?
qa.a: Nandita felt shocked and anxious, realising they had no childcare plan with only two months to go.

qa.q: What would you change first in how Siddharth and Nandita planned childcare?
qa.a: Ask the grandparents early instead of assuming, and list other options like a crèche or nanny with backups.

qa.q: How might Pankaj feel having to say no?
qa.a: Pankaj is sorry and uncomfortable, wanting to help but unable to because of his wife's health and their own home.

grounding: It shows a couple assuming the grandparents would move in to help, then scrambling with no plan when the grandparents say health and home make it difficult.

subtype: Approach: assuming grandparents will handle childcare [Pitfall]
passage:
Looking back, the biggest mistake Ravi and I made wasn't about money or hospitals. It was one assumption.
We never asked my mother, Vidya, if she would move in with us in Bengaluru after the baby. We just knew she would. She'd looked after my sister's children. Of course she'd do the same for ours.
When I was seven months along, I called her with dates. There was a long silence. Then: "Lakshmi, kanna, my blood pressure has been bad. The doctor says no big changes. And your father can't manage the house in Mysore alone."
I cried after that call. Not because she was wrong, but because we'd built our whole plan on her and never checked.
We spent the next month in a panic: visiting crèches, interviewing nannies, begging my manager for extra leave.
We managed. But it was frantic, and it didn't have to be.

qa.q: How did Lakshmi feel after the call with Vidya?
qa.a: Lakshmi felt upset and panicked, crying because their whole plan had rested on an assumption that was never checked.

qa.q: What else could Lakshmi and Ravi have done months earlier?
qa.a: They could have asked Vidya openly about her health and plans, and prepared crèche or nanny options as backups.

qa.q: How might Vidya have felt telling Lakshmi she couldn't come?
qa.a: Vidya probably felt sad and guilty, wanting to help but unable to because of her health and her husband's needs.

grounding: It shows a couple taking for granted that a grandparent would move in, then scrambling for childcare when her health and home made that difficult.
